Visitors ask this, and the honest answer is a fair sample of how Ziyang builds things,
so it is worth answering precisely.

The agent you are talking to runs **in your browser**. Not the UI around a server-side
agent — the harness itself: the tool-calling loop, the retrieval, the sub-agent spawning,
and the event stream this interface renders all execute in your tab. The page is a static
bundle on GitHub Pages; there is no application server.
chunks.about-this-site#1:
One thing cannot live in your browser: the model API key. A public bundle is readable by
anyone, so a key inside it would be extracted and drained. A single edge function holds
the key and does three things — forward a chat completion to DeepSeek, run a web search,
and fetch a URL — while validating that the request is one this site could plausibly have
made. It is a keyholder, not the agent.
chunks.about-this-site#2:
**Retrieval.** The corpus is built ahead of time from his résumé (English and Chinese),
his preprints on arXiv and Zenodo, and his own GitHub repositories and pull requests, chunked and indexed
into BM25. The index ships as a JSON file the page fetches on the first question. There
is no vector database and no embedding call at query time: on a corpus this size, lexical
retrieval with the model reformulating its own queries is both cheaper and easier to
debug than a similarity score nobody can read. The tokenizer emits Chinese unigrams and
bigrams, so the Chinese résumé is retrievable rather than one enormous token.
chunks.about-this-site#3:
**Tools.** `retrieve` (BM25 over the corpus), `read_document` (a whole section),
`web_search` and `fetch_url` (through the edge function), `github_activity` (the public
GitHub API, straight from the browser, no key), and `spawn_subagent` — a nested loop with
retrieval-only tools for reading in parallel without filling the main context window.

**What you can see.** Every reasoning step, tool call, argument and result is in the
collapsed activity line above each answer. Open it. The interface reports what the agent
did rather than asserting that it worked, which is the same reason the migration checker
in V2V OS compares disks block by block instead of trusting that the transfer said OK.
chunks.about-this-site#4:
**What is recorded.** The edge function writes one line per question to its runtime log:
the question text, the time, the country the request came from, and a short hash that stands
in for the visitor. The hash is salted with a server-side secret, so it cannot be turned back
into an address by anyone reading the logs. It exists so Ziyang can see what people ask this
page, which is the useful part. No account, no cookie, no analytics script, and no third party
receives any of it.

The design of this interface came from Claude's design tool; the harness behind it was
written for this site.

# ziyangliu-666.github.io

An agent that answers questions about Ziyang Liu. The harness runs in the visitor's
browser: the tool-calling loop, the retrieval, the sub-agents and the event stream all
execute in the tab. The page is a static bundle on GitHub Pages — there is no application
server.

One thing cannot run in the browser: the model API key. A public bundle is readable, so a
key inside it would be extracted. `proxy/` is three edge functions that hold the keys and
nothing else.

The previous Next.js site for this domain is preserved on the `archive/nextjs-site` branch
and tagged `v0-nextjs`.

## Layout
chunks.repo-ziyangliu-666.github.io#2:
```
src/ui/          The interface, ported from the Claude Design project. Renders events.
src/agent/       The harness: provider, loop, tools, prompts, event contract.
src/rag/         BM25 retrieval over the prebuilt corpus, and its tokenizer.
scripts/         Corpus builder and a retrieval debugger.
corpus/src/      Hand-written profile notes that go into the corpus.
content/blog/    Ziyang's posts. No pages any more; they are corpus material.
public/corpus/   Build output: the index and one JSON per document. Committed.
proxy/           Vercel edge functions holding the DeepSeek and Tavily keys.
```
chunks.repo-ziyangliu-666.github.io#3:
The seam between the interface and everything else is `src/agent/events.ts`: fourteen
event types, defined by the design. The UI renders that stream and owns no timing. Swap
the transport and the UI does not change — which is how the offline fallback and the live
harness share one component.

## Develop

```sh
npm install
npm run dev            # http://localhost:5173
```

With no model configured the site uses the offline transport: a handful of canned answers,
labelled as such. To talk to a real model, either point at a proxy —

```sh
echo 'VITE_AGENT_PROXY_URL=https://your-proxy.vercel.app' > .env.local
```

— or paste a DeepSeek key once in the browser console, which stores it in localStorage on
your machine only:
chunks.repo-ziyangliu-666.github.io#4:
```js

```

## The corpus

Built locally, committed, never built in CI — its sources are the résumé and paper PDFs,
which live outside the repository.

```sh
npm run corpus                                    # rebuild the index
npx tsx scripts/query-corpus.ts --self-test       # retrieval assertions
npx tsx scripts/query-corpus.ts "transfer throughput"
```

Sources, and the rule for each, are declared at the top of `scripts/build-corpus.ts`. Two
of them are load-bearing rather than incidental:
chunks.repo-ziyangliu-666.github.io#5:
- The **three arXiv preprints** and the **three mathematics preprints on Zenodo** are indexed
  in full. They are public. The Zenodo PDFs are saved in `~/Downloads` as

# gpu-segments

Several isolated processes that serve the same model on one GPU each load their own copy of the weights. gpu-segments loads the weights once. A broker process holds them in device memory, and each process maps that copy read-only.

The figure shows device memory, to scale, measured on one A100 40 GB with vLLM and Qwen2.5-1.5B, with replicas under load. Seven replicas that serve one trace use 28.9 GiB with private weights and 10.6 GiB with a shared segment, at the same throughput. The data and the experiments are in [elastic-gpu-research](https://github.com/ziyangliu-666/elastic-gpu-research), Results 33 to 40.

Isolation stays as it is:
chunks.repo-gpu-segments#2:
- Each process keeps its own CUDA context and uses NVIDIA's unmodified driver library.
- A fault stays in the process that caused it. A store into a segment faults the writer.
- The broker can run in another container or as another user.

## Running

Needs Linux, an NVIDIA driver, the CUDA headers (`CUDA=/usr/local/cuda` by default), gcc, and PyTorch.

```console
$ make
$ python3 -m gpu_segments --socket /run/segments.sock --file llama=/models/llama.safetensors
```

Only registered names can be opened. Clients cannot name a path.

```python
from gpu_segments import Client

c = Client("/run/segments.sock")
weights = c.open("llama")             # {tensor name: read-only CUDA tensor}
model.load_state_dict(weights, assign=True)
```
chunks.repo-gpu-segments#3:
## Park and resume

`c.park("llama")` unmaps the segment and frees the process's scratch memory. The tensors keep their addresses. `c.resume("llama")` maps the segment again at the same addresses, so the model needs no rebuild and no warm-up.

If the broker evicted the segment, `resume` waits while the broker loads it again, and returns True. If the file changed, the tensors then hold the new weights. If its layout changed, `resume` fails.

| step, 1.6 GB model, A100 | time |
|---|---:|
| park | 0.4 ms |
| resume, segment loaded | 1.3 ms |
| resume after eviction | about 120 ms |
chunks.repo-gpu-segments#4:
To free the context's device memory too (about 500 MiB for a PyTorch process on an A100), checkpoint the parked process with `cuda-checkpoint --toggle`. Restore took 121 ms on an RTX 3060 with `CUDA_DEVICE_MAX_CONNECTIONS=1`, and 229 ms without it.

## Memory budget

`--budget-gib 30` caps the device memory of all segments. To load a new one past the cap, the broker evicts the least recently used segments that no client maps. If every loaded segment is mapped, the open fails.

## Accounting

`Client.usage()` returns the device memory that the broker charges to each uid.
chunks.repo-gpu-segments#5:
- A segment that several uids map is split equally between them.
- A segment that is loaded but not mapped is charged to nobody, because the broker may evict it.
- The broker's uid and root see every uid. Other clients see only their own.

A scheduler can add this charge to the memory that a tenant's own contexts use.

## Broker restart

Mappings survive a broker crash: clients keep running on the memory they map. A client reconnects on its next call. After a restart, `resume` loads a fresh copy and returns True; the old copy is freed when the last client parks.

## Access
chunks.repo-gpu-segments#6:
- The socket is mode 0660 by default. `--allow-uid` adds uids that may open segments.
- Only the broker's uid and root may evict.
- An fd received from the broker grants read access to the segment. Do not pass it on.
- A segment works across containers. A gVisor sandbox needs a change in nvproxy: [google/gvisor#16898](https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/16898).

## Limits

- Weights must not change. Training needs ordinary memory.
- The broker refuses to evict a segment while any client maps it, because a later load would hold a second copy. `evict(force=True)` overrides this. A client that exits releases its mappings.
- The first load copies the file into pinned host memory, which stays allocated for later reloads.

# warmd

A shared CUDA context for short-lived processes.

The warmd daemon holds one CUDA context per GPU. Programs that load warmd's `libcuda.so.1` send their driver calls to it, so they can `fork()` after CUDA is initialized. Use it for many short tasks in one trust domain. All its processes share one fault domain.

To share model weights between processes that keep their own contexts, use [gpu-segments](https://github.com/ziyangliu-666/gpu-segments). It does not need warmd. For many short kernels in one trust domain, also compare with NVIDIA MPS: the measurements are in [elastic-gpu-research](https://github.com/ziyangliu-666/elastic-gpu-research).

## Building

Needs Linux x86-64, NVIDIA driver 550 or newer, CUDA headers, gcc and make.
chunks.repo-warmd#2:
```console
$ make
$ build/warmd &
$ LD_LIBRARY_PATH=build/lib python3 -c 'import torch; print(torch.ones(2, device="cuda"))'
```

`tests/run.sh` runs the tests.

## Performance

Short PyTorch tasks on an A100 (driver 570, 8 vCPUs), each in its own process:

| | 1 at a time | 8 at a time |
|---|---:|---:|
| native, fork after `import torch` | 2.1/s | 4.5/s |
| warmd, fork after `import torch` | 8.1/s | 59/s |
| warmd, fork after CUDA warm-up | 42/s | 133/s |

Each call to the daemon adds 10 to 15 µs, and large copies run at 3 to 5 GB/s. Details in
[docs/perf.md](docs/perf.md).

```
# paperstack

A Claude Code skill repository that turns Claude into a rigorous academic research partner — from first idea to final submission.

paperstack covers the full research lifecycle:

1. **Idea development**: Stress-test, sharpen, and frame your research ideas before committing months of work.
2. **Research workflows**: Study a topic through structured reading, adversarial critique, cross-paper comparison, and synthesis.
3. **Draft review**: Review your own paper before submission. Get conference-style feedback that exposes rejection risk.

## Why this exists

Most AI paper tools produce summaries. Summaries are not understanding — and summaries won't save you from Reviewer 2.
chunks.repo-paperstack#2:
Understanding requires you to state what you believe before reading, identify the weakest link in an argument, separate claims from evidence, and take a position you can defend. paperstack forces this discipline at every step.

Pre-submission review requires something harder: simulating the scrutiny of a hostile but fair reviewer who knows the field. paperstack's `/draft-review` does this by scanning your workspace, reading your full manuscript, and generating a conference-style review with verdict, major concerns, and a revision checklist.
```

# nullify

`nullify` is a Windows desktop installer for CS2 CFG setup, built with Tauri, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.

It helps users detect local Steam accounts, install the bundled CFG set, configure launch options for Steam or third-party platforms, and manage feature keybinds from a simple desktop UI.

## Overview

`nullify` is designed as a guided installer instead of a raw config pack. The app walks the user through:

- detecting available Steam accounts
- installing or uninstalling the bundled CFG files
- applying the correct launch flow for Steam or third-party platforms
- configuring bhop, jump throw, jumpbug, and related binds
- closing the setup once everything is ready

## Features
chunks.repo-nullify#2:
- Detect local Steam accounts
- Install or uninstall CFG files
- Guide launch option setup for Steam and third-party platforms
- Configure bhop, jump throw, jumpbug, and related keybinds

## Requirements

- Windows
- Node.js
- Rust / Cargo

## Quick Start

```bash
cd app
npm install
```

## Development

```bash
cd app
npm run tauri dev
```

## Build

```bash
cd app
npm run tauri build
```

The packaged desktop output is produced by Tauri under the build artifacts generated from `app/src-tauri`.

## Project Layout

- `app/`: frontend and Tauri application
- `cfg/`: generated and bundled CFG files
- `tools/`: helper generation scripts
- `docs/`: README assets

## License

MIT

# PawMemo

A terminal vocabulary companion — with character.
Capture words in context. Review with FSRS. Get nagged by a companion who has opinions about your study habits.

--- ## Review cards, not flashcard apps
chunks.repo-pawmemo#2:
PawMemo shows you a word in its original context and asks you to recall the meaning. When you're ready, peek the answer — then rate it honestly.

Four ratings: **Again · Hard · Good · Easy**. The scheduler (FSRS-style, stability-aware) decides when you see it next. All state lives in a local SQLite file — nothing leaves your machine. --- ## A companion that stays in character
chunks.repo-pawmemo#3: The companion layer sits on top of the study engine. It can change tone, copy, and presentation — but it cannot change your review schedule or your word state. Three built-in packs: | Pack | Character | Tone | |------|-----------|------| | `momo` | Momo | Calm, minimal | | `girlfriend` | Mina | Present, warm | | `tsundere` | Airi | She's doing you a favor | ```bash pawmemo config companion --pack tsundere ``` Airi makes her feelings known: ``` (｀_´) 哦，你终于来了。别在那打招呼了，赶紧把剩下的4个复习完， 我可没时间一直陪你耗着。 ``` --- ## Study progress, always local

---

## Install

```bash
npm install && npm run build && npm link
```

Or from the packed tarball:

```bash
npm pack
npm install -g ./pawmemo-0.1.0.tgz
```

**Configure an LLM provider** (used for `ask`, `teach`, and companion chat):

```bash
pawmemo config llm use --provider openai --model gpt-4o-mini --api-key "sk-..."
```

---

```bash
# Save a word with context
pawmemo capture ephemeral --ctx "The beauty of the moment was ephemeral." --gloss "lasting a very short time"

# Ask your companion to explain it
pawmemo ask ephemeral --ctx "The beauty of the moment was ephemeral."

# Open the shell
pawmemo
```

# EasyTrainer
[🔎Chinese documentation](https://github.com/comethx/EasyTrainer/blob/main/README_CN.md)

Quickly train and invoke a machine learning image classification model with **a few lines of code**.

```python
from EasyTrainerCore import EasyTrain

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = EasyTrain.start()
    img = Image.open("your image path")
    result = model.predict(img)
```

This project is a further encapsulation of Pytorch and is aimed at helping beginners of deep learning. My purpose is to reduce the time for debugging code, so that everyone can focus on model tuning and participate in optimization strategy selection.

## Getting started

### Environment preparation

First clone this repository

chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#0:
# Architecture

The engine thread holds the books, orders, positions and risk state; venue threads feed it through single-producer, single-consumer rings, and it journals each message it consumes. Live sessions, backtests and replays build the same engine with a different clock, feed and transport. The overview with an animation is [How FastMM works](how-it-works.md).
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#1: `fastmm-live` runs a fixed set of threads for the whole session:
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#2:
| Thread | Owns | Waits by |
|---|---|---|
| `fm-net-<i>`, one per venue | the network reactor: sockets, TLS, WebSocket and HTTP, decoding, book sync, order encoding and signing, the rate limiter, the order latency histograms | `epoll_wait` or `io_uring_enter` (`[engine] net_backend`), or busy |
| `fm-engine` | books, strategy, risk, OMS, quote manager, timers, positions, journal sequencing | busy spin, or a futex with `spin_mode = "adaptive"` |
| journal writer | the journal ring into the `.fmj` file; runs when journaling is on | spin, then waits of 50 µs to 1 ms |
| `fm-store` | fill, order, position, kill and funding rows; runs unless `[storage] backend = "none"` | 2 ms sleeps when idle |
| log sink | every thread's log records | spin, then waits of 50 µs to 10 ms |
| main | configuration, thread start and stop, the control socket, signals, the engine's heartbeat | `poll`, at most 50 ms |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#3:
The main thread also keeps time-driven work off the engine:

| Every | Main thread work |
|---|---|
| 250 ms | writes the status file and the kill file |
| 1 s | posts the venues' timers and prints the stats line |
| `[engine] tsc_recalibrate_s` | recalibrates the clock ([Clock calibration](#clock-calibration)) |
| SIGINT, SIGTERM, `--duration` | sets the kill switch, then cancels all orders on each venue over a separate REST connection |

With `spin_mode = "adaptive"` nothing spins while idle. A network thread polls while active and for 200 µs after, then waits with a 1 ms timeout. The engine spins, then sleeps on a futex that the network threads signal, at most until the next timer.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#4:
Every ring has one producer and one consumer, so N producers mean N rings. The engine visits them round-robin, at most 64 messages per ring per visit, and the journal records events in the order the engine consumed them.

With `fastmm-live --gateway <socket>` there are no `fm-net-<i>` threads. The venues run in `fastmm-gateway`, and each venue's rings live in shared memory with the same protocol ([Run behind a gateway](../how-to/operations/run-behind-a-gateway.md)).
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#5:
`[engine] threading = "single"` removes `fm-net-0`: the pinned engine thread runs the venue's network loop before every engine step. No event crosses a core between the packet read and the order write. It takes one venue; a configuration with more is refused.

| Event | With `threading = "single"` |
|---|---|
| market data | journaled, applied and handed to the strategy while the venue is still in the receive callback that decoded it |
| outbound orders | encoded and written in one call from the engine thread, so tick-to-trade ends with the order on the socket |
| order events, control messages, timers | taken by the step after each network iteration |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#6: The rings stay, as same-thread queues, and the journal records the same order of events, so replay works unchanged. The cost: while the engine works nobody reads the sockets, and a slow strategy hook delays the venue's heartbeats too. Numbers: [Benchmarks](benchmarks.md).
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#7: Every connection runs on a single-threaded event loop with a timer heap and a mailbox that other threads may post to. One iteration waits for I/O until the next timer, dispatches it, then runs posted tasks and expired timers, without allocating. `[engine] net_backend` picks the backend for `fastmm-live` and `fastmm-sim-exchange`:
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#8:
| | `epoll` (default) | `io_uring` |
|---|---|---|
| registration | `epoll_ctl`, edge-triggered | one multishot poll per descriptor |
| wait | `epoll_wait`, timeout in whole ms | `io_uring_enter`, timeout in ns |
| busy poll | `epoll_wait` with a zero timeout | reads the completion ring in user space, enters the kernel only to submit |
| needs | any kernel | Linux 5.13 or newer, not blocked by `kernel.io_uring_disabled` or seccomp |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#9:
When io_uring is unavailable, `fastmm-live` and the simulator log a warning and use epoll. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks it. The two backends are within measurement noise of each other on a loopback echo ([bench/full-results.md](../../bench/full-results.md)): the `read` and `write` calls dominate, and io_uring saves only the empty wait of a busy-polling loop.

Code that registers its own descriptors, as a new venue does, follows three rules:
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#10:
| Rule | Because |
|---|---|
| `remove()` before `close()` | an io_uring poll holds the file open, so a closed socket would stay bound until the poll is cancelled |
| tolerate a spurious readiness call | a multishot poll reports every wake-up; the extra read or write returns EAGAIN |
| expect a removed handler not to be called | the handler is looked up again for each event in a batch |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#11:
The engine reserves all its memory before the first event and touches each slot once, so no page fault lands in the middle of trading. In the engine benchmark a book update becomes an order in 143 ns (p50) ([Benchmarks](benchmarks.md)).

<video class="fastmm-video" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata" poster="../../assets/anim/reserved-at-startup.jpg" src="../../assets/anim/reserved-at-startup.mp4"></video>
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#12:
| Reserved | Capacity |
|---|---|
| open orders | 4,096 |
| instruments: books, positions, risk state | 256 |
| orders sent per event | 32 |
| market-data ring per venue | 4 MiB, `[engine] md_ring_bytes` |
| order-event ring per venue | 1 MiB, `[engine] order_ring_bytes` |
| journal ring | 16 MiB, `[engine] journal_ring_bytes` |

While trading, an order takes a free slot and gives it back when it is done. A usual program asks the allocator, and sometimes the kernel, for each new order:

<video class="fastmm-video" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata" poster="../../assets/anim/no-allocation.jpg" src="../../assets/anim/no-allocation.mp4"></video>
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#13:
1. No heap allocation after warm-up; `tests/hotpath` counts every global `operator new` and fails on one.
2. No exceptions: hot functions return `Result<T, E>` and are `noexcept` ([ADR-0002](../adr/0002-exceptions-off-hot-path.md)).
3. No `double` in price and quantity arithmetic: they are `int64` with a 1e-8 scale ([Fixed point](../reference/fixed-point.md)).
4. No virtual calls in the engine loop: strategy, clock, transport and feed are template parameters ([ADR-0009](../adr/0009-crtp-strategies-over-virtual.md)). Run-to-completion adds one indirect call per market-data event and one per outbound batch.
5. Every message between threads is trivially copyable with an explicit size.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#14: A strategy is built through a registry that keeps one factory per transport: simulated, replay and live. A strategy library registers its strategies with one function that calls `register_strategy<S>(r)` for each. The command lines register the built-in strategies and then the modules the program passes; a factory no file compiles is a link error ([Register a strategy](../how-to/strategies/register-a-strategy.md)).
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#15: The live clock reads the CPU's time-stamp counter and converts it to wall-clock ns with a measured rate and an anchor. The first rate comes from a 50 ms measurement against `CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW`; the anchor is `CLOCK_REALTIME`.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#16:
| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| recalibration | every `[engine] tsc_recalibrate_s` (default 10 s, 0 off), the main thread measures the rate over the whole time since the last anchor, so clock jitter costs a few ppm |
| log | `tsc recalibrated: drift <ns> over <s> (<ppm>) ...` |
| hand-over | the engine picks up the new calibration once per loop iteration, with one atomic load when nothing changed |
| small offset | the clock stays continuous and slews the offset away over one period, at most 500 ppm |
| offset over 1 ms | the clock steps to the measurement, counts `clock_steps` and logs a warning |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#17:
The calibration follows `CLOCK_REALTIME`, so when the host steps its wall clock the engine clock steps with it. NTP corrections and WSL2 resyncing with Windows do that, sometimes by hundreds of milliseconds.

| CPU flags in `/proc/cpuinfo` | Wall time | Latency intervals |
|---|---|---|
| `constant_tsc` and `nonstop_tsc` | the calibrated counter | counter cycles at the measured rate |
| `constant_tsc` only, as on many KVM cloud instances | `clock_gettime`, no recalibration | counter cycles at the measured rate |
| neither | `clock_gettime`, no recalibration | `clock_gettime` ns |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#18:
Each stamp is a counter reading; intervals go into allocation-free log-linear histograms.

| Stamp | Thread | Taken when |
|---|---|---|
| T0 | network | the frame was received |
| T1 | network | it was decoded into an engine message |
| T2 | engine | the book, position or OMS was updated |
| T3 | engine | the strategy hook returned |
| T4, T5 | engine | around the hand-over of the outbound batch: a ring push, or with `threading = "single"` the encoding and write |

The engine publishes decode, book apply, strategy, serialize (T3 to T4), send (T4 to T5), tick-to-trade (T0 to T5) and wire-to-book (T0 to T2) every `latency_publish_ms`. Each outbound order carries its trigger's T0, and the network thread measures the rest:
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#19:
| Interval | Measures |
|---|---|
| encode | JSON encoding and signing |
| send | the WebSocket or REST send call |
| wire tick-to-trade | T0 to after the send; orders from timers are not counted |

`fastmm-live` prints the wire tick-to-trade p50 and p99 and the encode and send p50 per venue in its stats line and final summary.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-architecture#20:
| Failure | Detection | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Market-data disconnect | EPOLLRDHUP, a read of 0 bytes, a TLS error | quotes pulled, reconnect with backoff, fresh snapshot |
| Sequence gap | the book sync state machine | quotes pulled, re-snapshot (rate limited) |
| Stale feed | no traffic for the connector's `stale_ms` | quotes pulled; `dead_ms` without traffic forces a reconnect ([Venue connectors](../reference/venues.md#configuration-keys)) |
| Order channel loss | the connection state machine | cancel-all over REST (`cancel_on_order_channel_loss`); after reconnect, replay executions, then reconcile open orders |
| Kill switch | `max_loss`, a full ring, every venue killed, a strategy error, client order ids used up, a signal, `--duration`, a journal write failure | stop quoting and cancel working orders; at shutdown each venue cancels all over REST, 5 s timeout ([Risk model](risk-model.md#the-kill-switch), [Kill switch and shutdown](../how-to/operations/kill-switch-and-shutdown.md)) |
| Venue unusable | a fatal error such as a bad key or signature, Binance HTTP 418, a dead man's switch not refreshed, a multicast feed that cannot rebuild | that venue's kill switch; every venue killed is a global kill |
| Rate limit | response headers and error codes | cool down until the limit resets; after HTTP 418 REST stays stopped until restart |
| Clock skew | timestamp rejection codes | re-measure the offset from the venue's time endpoint |
| Engine thread stuck | its heartbeat has not moved for `[engine] stall_ms` | cancel-all on every venue from the main thread, exit code 5 ([Engine stall](../how-to/operations/kill-switch-and-shutdown.md#engine-stall)) |
| Ring overflow | a push fails | market data: drop the delta and resync; order events: kill switch |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#0:
# Event flow

One market-data update in `fastmm-live` travels from the venue's socket to an order on the wire, and its fill comes back into the strategy. Backtests and replays run the same engine with a simulated clock, feed and transport ([Determinism](determinism.md)); threads and rings are in [Architecture](architecture.md).
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#1:
The network thread reads the socket, decrypts TLS, unframes WebSocket messages and parses the venue's JSON into fixed-size messages. It stamps the receive time (T0) before parsing and the decode time (T1) after.

| Connection | Messages |
|---|---|
| market data | `BookDeltaMsg` (snapshot or delta), `TradeMsg`, `BookTickerMsg` |
| user stream | `OrderAckMsg`, `OrderFillMsg` and the other order events |

The book-sync state machine aligns the REST snapshot with the delta stream by the venue's sequence numbers. A gap puts the book into `Resyncing` and fetches a new snapshot; a connection silent for `stale_ms` is reported `Stale`.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#2: `nasdaq_itch` has no TLS or JSON; the receive side is UDP lines A and B, MoldUDP64, ITCH and an L3 book, and orders go out through OUCH.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#3:
1. The network thread takes a batch of datagrams from the kernel or an AF_XDP ring and stamps T0 once per batch. The kernel's receive time is recorded too.
2. MoldUDP64 takes the first copy of each packet from line A or B, holds packets ahead of a gap and re-requests the missing ones.
3. Each ITCH message updates the instrument's L3 book; after each datagram the changed top levels go out as one `BookDeltaMsg` per instrument (T1).
4. A gap that cannot be recovered puts the venue into `Resyncing` until a GLIMPSE snapshot rebuilds the books ([Venue connectors](../reference/venues/nasdaq-itch.md#startup-and-recovery)).
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#4:
Messages cross to the engine through single-producer, single-consumer rings: market data and order events per venue, plus the control ring. The engine visits them round-robin, at most `[engine] max_events_per_step` (default 64) per ring, then runs due timers.

| Ring full | Result |
|---|---|
| market data | the delta is dropped and the book resyncs |
| order events | the kill switch ends the session; order events are never dropped |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#5: For each event the engine reads its clock once, which is `ctx.now()` for the hooks. It records the event in the journal with that time, then dispatches on its type.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#7: The hook reads what it needs through `ctx` and usually calls `ctx.set_quotes(id, quotes)` with up to 8 levels per side. The call returns at once (T3); nothing has been sent yet.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#8:
The quote manager compares each wanted level with the order resting in the same slot:

| Decision | When |
|---|---|
| keep | the price is within `min_requote_ticks` and the remaining quantity covers `min_qty_bps` of the wanted one, or the slot changed less than `min_requote_interval_ms` ago |
| replace | the venue supports it and `supports_replace` is on |
| cancel, then new | otherwise; the new order goes out once the cancel is acknowledged, and is withheld if the old order filled instead and the balance no longer covers it |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#9: An order waiting for a venue response is left alone until it arrives. A side whose new order or replace the venue, the price collar or the fat-finger band refused pauses for `reject_backoff_ms`, then quotes again ([Venue-originated rejects](../reference/errors.md#venue-originated)). Orders sent directly with `ctx.send` skip this step.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#10: Each new order and replace passes the pre-trade checks ([Risk model](risk-model.md)). A passing order enters the OMS as `PendingNew` with a client order id made of the session epoch and a sequence number, and joins the event's outbound batch.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#11:
When the event is handled, the engine hands the batch over (T4 to T5). Live, that is a push to the venue's outbound ring and a wake-up of the network thread; in a backtest, the simulated venue's queue. The journal keeps a copy of each message.

The network thread encodes the order in the venue's format, signs it and writes it to the WebSocket API or REST connection. It records the wire tick-to-trade latency from T0.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#12: The acknowledgement or fill comes back on the user stream and takes steps 1 to 3 through the order ring. The OMS applies the transition, for example `PendingNew` to `Live`, and the quote manager updates the slot. For a fill, the engine books the position and fees, checks `max_loss`, calls `on_fill(ctx, fill)` and then `on_order_update(ctx, u)`.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-event-flow#13:
| Event | What the engine does |
|---|---|
| timer | fires from a timer wheel in engine time, between events; journaled as a `Timer` message, then `on_timer` |
| connection change | for any state but `Live`, pulls the venue's quotes, clears its books for market data, then calls `on_connection` |
| order channel reconnect | the connector replays executions since the last one booked, then reconciles open orders and positions; quotes pause until it ends |
| funding payment | booked as realized PnL of the perpetual and checked against `max_loss`; no hook |
| quoting switched on or off | `on_quoting`, after the event or timer that changed it |
| shutdown | kill switch through the engine, then cancel-all on each venue over REST ([Kill switch and shutdown](../how-to/operations/kill-switch-and-shutdown.md)) |

chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-determinism#0:
# Determinism

A backtest with the same inputs sends the same orders, and replaying a journal sends the same order messages as the session that wrote it. `fastmm-replay --verify` checks the second property by comparing the SHA-256 of both outbound streams ([How it is checked](#how-it-is-checked)).
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-determinism#1:
| Use | How |
|---|---|
| debugging a live session | replay its journal under a debugger, without a venue, and the same decisions run again |
| catching regressions | golden hashes in the tests fail when a change alters what a strategy sends |
| comparing parameter sets | two backtests differ only by their parameters |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-determinism#2: `Engine<Strategy, Clock, Transport, Feed>` takes the sources of non-determinism as compile-time policies:
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-determinism#3:
| Input | Live | Backtest | Replay |
|---|---|---|---|
| clock | `TscClock` (CPU counter calibrated against wall time) | `SimClock`, driven by event times | `SimClock`, set to the recorded engine clock |
| events | `RingFeed` from the network threads | `InlineFeed` from the data source or generator | `JournalFeed` in recorded order |
| orders | `LiveTransport` to the venue | `SimTransport`: matching engine with a seeded latency model | `ReplayTransport`: hashes and verifies what is sent, refuses what the recording refused; acks come from the journal |
| randomness | `ctx.rng()` seeded from `[engine] rng_seed` | the same | the seed from the journal header |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-determinism#4:
The rest is deterministic by construction: one engine thread, no reads of the system clock, integer arithmetic for money, containers iterated in a defined order and timers that fire in engine time.

Operator actions are inputs too. Commands on the control socket ([Operate a running session](../how-to/operations/operate-a-running-session.md)) reach the engine through a journaled ring, and a flatten runs on a journaled timer. A replay of an incident reproduces the pull, the new limits and every reduce-only order the flatten sent.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-determinism#5: A live session is not repeatable, because network timing decides which event comes first, but its journal is. The journal records the engine clock of every event and timer, and in its header the session epoch, the quoting state, each venue's cancel-replace setting, the configuration and the strategy's parameter table ([Journal format](../reference/journal-format.md)). Replay restores all of them.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-determinism#6:
`fastmm-replay --verify` (or `tutorial-replay`, or any app built with `cli::replay`) compares every outbound order message the replayed engine sends with the copy in the journal and prints the SHA-256 of both streams:

```text
recorded outbound 712 msgs sha256 1116a9bd...
replayed outbound 712 msgs sha256 1116a9bd...
replay MATCH
```

On a mismatch it prints the first differing message as recorded and as replayed and exits with code 1. Only the first difference means anything: replay feeds the recorded acknowledgements whatever it sent, so later messages diverge too.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-determinism#7:
| Cause | Why | Instead |
|---|---|---|
| Reading the system clock (`std::chrono::system_clock`, `clock_gettime`) in a hook | replay runs at a different wall time | `ctx.now()` |
| `std::random_device`, an unseeded or time-seeded generator | a different sequence on every run | `ctx.rng()` |
| State kept outside the strategy object (static or global variables, a counter shared by two strategies) | survives from one run to the next in the same process, as in sweeps or tests | members of the strategy |
| Reading files, environment variables or the network from a hook | not an engine input, not journaled | parameters, read once at configuration |
| Logic that depends on logs, or on `EngineStats` latency figures | logs are not journaled; wall-clock latencies differ | engine state visible through `ctx` |
| Threads or asynchronous work started by the strategy | results arrive at an unrecorded time | do the work in a hook, or publish results as engine events |
| Uninitialised members, iteration over pointer-keyed hash maps | values or order change between runs | initialise every member; order by ids |
| Floating-point decisions that differ between builds (`-ffast-math`, a different compiler, `-march=native`) | the same inputs round differently | fixed-point arithmetic for prices and sizes; replay with the binary that recorded |
| A different binary: changed strategy or engine code, other parameters | the decisions differ | a replay with `--config` or `--strategy` is reported as a what-if run |
| A journal written before format version 2, from a live session | it has no engine clock or session settings | replay with `--config` as a what-if run |
| A full journal ring during recording | events were lost; the engine trips the kill switch | size `[engine] journal_ring_bytes` for the session |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-determinism#8: A mismatch with the same binary and the embedded configuration is a bug: some code read an input the journal does not record.

# Benchmarks

The results and the machine are on [Benchmarks](../docs/explanation/benchmarks.md); every benchmark is in [full-results.md](full-results.md). `scripts/bench.sh` regenerates both and this file.

```bash
scripts/bench-e2e.sh --duration 30 --runs 3 --sim-cpu 0 --engine-cpu 1 --net-cpu 3 --out bench/results/e2e
./scripts/bench.sh --preset release-native --cpu 1 --rounds 3 --e2e bench/results/e2e
python3 tools/check_budgets.py bench/results/latest
python3 tools/bench_compare.py bench/results/baseline bench/results/latest
```
chunks.fastmm-bench-readme#1:
`check_budgets.py` fails when a benchmark exceeds its budget in `bench/ci_budget.toml` by more than 10 %. `scripts/build-pgo.sh [--bolt]` builds `release-native` with PGO, and BOLT, trained on these benchmarks; shipped builds do not use it.

For an ITCH change, also replay a real session: NASDAQ publishes full days of TotalView-ITCH 5.0 (`emi.nasdaq.com/ITCH`). `fastmm-bench-l3-itch` times every book message, `--from 09:30` times the open on books warmed by the morning, and `--check` compares every touch with a map book. `BM_ItchL2Bridge_Message_MultiSymbol` interleaves 1, 10 and 100 books, so a datagram publishes several of them.

```bash
build/release/bin/bench/fastmm-bench-l3-itch day.itch --top 100 --from 09:30 --check
```
chunks.fastmm-bench-readme#2: For a change to the queue models, `fastmm-bench-queue-truth` scores `l2_queue` and `l3_queue` against the same file, where every order's outcome is known ([below](#queue-models-against-itch)).
chunks.fastmm-bench-readme#3:
`scripts/bench.sh` pins each benchmark to one core, except the few that need a second thread (`FASTMM_BENCH_NEEDS_CORES`, `bench/bench_pin.hpp`). The machine ran nothing else, without `isolcpus` or a fixed CPU frequency. Each benchmark ran five repetitions in each of three rounds, and `tools/bench_table.py` pools them.

Where a benchmark keeps a per-operation `rdtsc` histogram (buckets about 2 % wide), the tables give its percentiles; otherwise p50 is the median over repetitions of Google Benchmark's mean time. The codec benchmarks time 64 operations per `rdtsc` pair. Two processes of one binary differ by 2 to 5 %, so compare a change over several interleaved processes per side.
chunks.fastmm-bench-readme#4: Tick to order (`BM_TickToOrder_Sim`) starts when a book delta is pushed into the engine's feed and ends when the last order it caused is serialised into the transport. In the simulator the transport copies each message into a 192-byte scheduler slot, the stand-in for the live engine's outbound ring. The venue, acks and the untimed settle loop between ticks are outside it. The simulator's outbound SHA-256, a determinism check the live engine does not compute, is off; `BM_TickToOrder_SimHash` turns it on.
chunks.fastmm-bench-readme#5: `scripts/bench-e2e.sh` runs `fastmm-sim-itch` and `fastmm-live` in two network namespaces joined by a veth pair: preset `release`, `configs/nasdaq-itch-sim.toml`, kernel receive, `spin_mode = "busy"`, simulator on CPU 0, engine on CPU 1, network thread on CPU 3 (the engine core's second hyperthread), three runs of 30 s.
chunks.fastmm-bench-readme#6: Wire to wire is measured by the simulator with its own TSC: from right before the `sendmmsg` that sent an ITCH datagram to right after the read that returned the order it caused. Each order carries the MoldUDP64 sequence number that triggered it in its ClOrdID, so the simulator matches them. `fastmm-live` measures the other rows from its T0 to T5 stamps. On veth the order's `write` runs the simulator's TCP receive path inside the system call, which is most of the gap between T5 and wire to wire.
chunks.fastmm-bench-readme#7: The numbers are on [Sweep performance](../docs/explanation/sweep-performance.md). Builds use gcc 13.3 and the preset `release-nolto`; each row is one run on an otherwise idle machine. The ITCH file is the day's file reduced to the messages of AAPL, MSFT, AMZN, FB, INTC, CSCO, NVDA and TSLA (186 MB, 6.1 million of its 282 million messages). The BTCUSDT configuration runs 5 ms latency with 2 ms jitter and our orders in the feed; `xmm` adds 15 ms to Bybit; ITCH runs 50 µs with our orders not in the feed.
chunks.fastmm-bench-readme#8: `fastmm-bench-multiverse` builds the variants (the configuration's own first, then the grid in a fixed shuffled order) and runs them through `bt::run_multiverse` as a sweep's points. With `--check K` it runs K of them, spread over the list, through `run_backtest()`, times them and compares each result field by field with `bt::result_difference`; any difference fails the run. "A variant in the pass" is the pass's wall time times its threads over its variants; "Against alone" divides the checked backtests' mean time by it. Memory is the process's peak resident set (`/usr/bin/time -f %M`).

| Binance USDⓈ-M BTCUSDT, 2026-09-01 00:00 to 04:00 UTC, Tardis book and trades | `l2_queue` | 939,569 events | 3.3 s |
| The same with Bybit BTCUSDT | `l2_queue` | 1,643,662 events | 4.4 s |
| Nasdaq TotalView-ITCH, 2019-07-30 09:30 to 16:00, 8 large stocks, every order | `l3_queue` | 5,353,515 events | 3.6 s |

The configurations are [`configs/backtest-binance.toml`](../../configs/backtest-binance.toml), [`configs/backtest-xmm.toml`](../../configs/backtest-xmm.toml) and [`configs/backtest-itch.toml`](../../configs/backtest-itch.toml). Fetching the data: [Market-data sources](../reference/data-sources.md#tardis).

Each row is one pass of 64 variants on one thread, against a backtest of its own per variant. The variants are a grid over the strategy's parameters and the order latency.

| Data | Strategy | A variant in the pass | Against alone |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| BTCUSDT | `basic_mm`, our orders in the feed | 137 ms | 24x |
| BTCUSDT | `basic_mm`, our orders not in the feed | 90 ms | 37x |
| BTCUSDT | `avellaneda_stoikov`, our orders in the feed | 195 ms | 17x |
| BTCUSDT on Binance and Bybit | `xmm`, quoting on Binance and hedging on Bybit | 386 ms | 11x |
| BTCUSDT | the `fastmm init` strategy, `@fastmm.hot` hooks | 158 ms | 20x |
| ITCH | `basic_mm`, 1-tick requote | 502 ms | 7x |
| ITCH | `avellaneda_stoikov` | 931 ms | 4x |

A strategy that declares the mid band it watches is handed a book only when the mid leaves it. The `fastmm init` strategy does, and costs about what `basic_mm` does. Without its band it took 248 ms a variant, 13x, because its hook ran for each of the 939,569 messages in every variant.

Share of a pass's time, from `perf record -g` of the passes above:

| | BTCUSDT `basic_mm` | ITCH `basic_mm`, 1-tick requote |
|---|---:|---:|
| Reading, ordering and applying the data to the shared books, once a pass | 44 % | 8 % |
| Engines handling market data: strategy, risk, OMS | 9 % | 28 % |
| The venue taking orders and the recorded events that reach them | 14 % | 20 % |
| Engines taking acks, cancel acks and fills | 14 % | 16 % |
| Keeping the runs in step | 9 % | 20 % |

On BTCUSDT most of the time is the pass's own, which more variants spread thinner. On ITCH a 1-tick requote sends up to 260,000 replaces a day per variant. Each is a strategy decision, a trip through risk and the OMS, a place in the venue's queue and two order events back.

1,024 BTCUSDT variants of `basic_mm` on the server:

| Threads | Wall | Speed-up | Peak memory |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 196.0 s | 1.0 | 1.5 GB |
| 2 | 86.9 s | 2.3 | 2.3 GB |
| 4 | 43.2 s | 4.5 | 3.9 GB |
| 8 | 22.0 s | 8.9 | 7.0 GB |
| 16 | 12.2 s | 16.1 | 7.0 GB |
| 32 | 7.1 s | 27.5 | 7.1 GB |
| 48 | 5.6 s | 34.9 | 7.2 GB |
| 64 | 4.9 s | 40.0 | 7.2 GB |

Two threads gain more than twice because a pass holds at most 128 points. One thread runs the 1,024 points in 8 waves and reads the data 8 times; two threads need 4. Each pass also keeps its own books, about 2 s of work however few points it holds, which is 40 % of the time at 64 threads. The desktop took 24.1 s on 8 threads.

A run's engine and venue take about 6 MB, so a sweep on 8 threads holds at most 1,024 runs, about 7 GB. A result keeps its fills and equity bars but no order rows. `fastmm-backtest --sweep` of BTCUSDT `basic_mm` on 8 threads; a point is the wall time times 8 threads over the points:

| Points | Wall | A point | Peak memory |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 | 2.4 s | 1,180 ms | 0.25 GB |
| 128 | 2.7 s | 170 ms | 1.0 GB |
| 1,024 | 17.1 s | 134 ms | 6.8 GB |
| 4,096 | 57.9 s | 113 ms | 6.9 GB |
| 16,384 | 228 s | 111 ms | 7.7 GB |

Up to 1,024 points the sweep is one wave of 8 passes, each paying about 2 s for its books. Past that, each wave pays it again, and a point costs what its own run costs.

A [shadow sweep](../how-to/operations/shadow-sweeps.md) over 2.5 hours of a recorded session on several venues, reading it as fast as it can, on the desktop. `basic_mm` requotes at every tick on every instrument, so it works much harder than a session that rests its quotes.

| Points | Threads | CPU per market-data event per point | Core time per session-hour per point | Memory per point | Session pace per thread |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1 | 2,682 ns | 7.5 s | 56 MB | 478 times |
| 8 | 1 | 1,987 ns | 5.6 s | 17 MB | 80 times |
| 32 | 1 | 3,662 ns | 10.3 s | 12 MB | 11 times |
| 128 | 2 | 8,131 ns | 22.9 s | 11 MB | 2.5 times |

The time per point grows with the points of a pass: their engines no longer fit the caches together. One point's row holds what all the points share, the reading of the journal.

Memory stays flat over the session: a point holds its current window. Reproduce it with `fastmm-bench-shadow --journal <first part> --strategy basic_mm --points 8` ([`bench/shadow_load.cpp`](../../bench/shadow_load.cpp)); `--compare` prints how many events of the stream differ from those of a finished journal's.

FastMM runs no part of a sweep on a GPU, for three reasons:

| Obstacle | Why |
|---|---|
| Divergent branches | each run takes each event through branches that differ from run to run, which a GPU warp runs one after another |
| Round trip per step | each step decides the next, so handing a GPU part of every step costs 12 µs on an H100, against 0.1 to 0.2 µs a run spends on an event on the CPU |
| Two engines | running whole runs on a GPU needs a second engine for every strategy |

A `basic_mm` kernel that holds a variant in a few hundred bytes shows what a GPU gains on the same work. Its outputs equal the CPU's bit for bit:

| Code | Hardware | 1,024 variants | 8,192 variants |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| The engine, any strategy | desktop, 8 threads | 72.9 s | |
| | server, 64 threads | 12.7 s | |
| `basic_mm` kernel, CPU | desktop, 8 threads | 5.8 s | 35.2 s |
| | server, 64 threads | 5.9 s | 9.3 s |
| `basic_mm` kernel, GPU | RTX 3090 | 3.5 s | 17.0 s |
| | H100 | 2.3 s | 7.6 s |

The RTX 3090 ran 1.6 and 2.1 times as fast as the desktop's 8 cores, the H100 2.6 and 1.2 times as fast as the server's 64 cores. Preparing the GPU's input takes another 4.2 to 4.6 s on one core. Counting it, only the RTX 3090 on 8,192 variants comes out ahead.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-how-it-works#0:
# How FastMM works

One thread makes every trading decision, and every event it acts on is recorded first. The rest of the program feeds that thread or writes down what it did.

<video class="fastmm-video" controls preload="none" poster="../../assets/film-poster.jpg" src="https://github.com/ziyangliu-666/FastMM/releases/download/v0.5.1/fastmm-film.mp4"></video>
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-how-it-works#1:
Books, orders, positions, risk limits and timers live on the engine thread, and no other thread touches them. The decision path takes no locks, and a session can be replayed from its recording.

<video class="fastmm-video" autoplay loop muted playsinline preload="metadata" poster="../../assets/anim/architecture.jpg" src="../../assets/anim/architecture.mp4"></video>

Each venue gets a network thread; behind one venue several accounts can trade. The network threads talk to the engine through queues with one writer and one reader each:
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-how-it-works#2:
| Thread | Does | Queue to the engine |
|---|---|---|
| network, one per venue | sockets, TLS, WebSocket, decoding, book sync, order encoding and signing | market data and order events in, orders out |
| engine | applies events, runs the strategy, turns quotes into orders, checks risk | |
| journal | appends every event the engine consumed to the `.fmj` file | the journal queue |
| store | writes fills, orders, positions and kills to the trade store | the record queue |
| log | formats and writes log lines | one queue per thread |
| main | configuration, start and stop, the control socket, the status file, signals | the control queue |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-how-it-works#3:
The engine takes at most 64 messages from one queue before moving to the next, so one busy venue cannot starve another. Two variants change the layout:

| Setting | Effect |
|---|---|
| `[engine] threading = "single"` | one venue only; the engine thread also runs the network loop, so nothing crosses a core between the packet and the order |
| `fastmm-live --gateway` | the network threads run in `fastmm-gateway`, and the queues are in shared memory ([Run behind a gateway](../how-to/operations/run-behind-a-gateway.md)) |

The thread table with how each thread waits is in [Architecture](architecture.md#threads).
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-how-it-works#4:
1. The network thread reads the socket, decodes the message and stamps its receive time.
2. It pushes the message to the engine's queue.
3. The engine reads its clock once and records the event in the journal.
4. It applies the event. A book update moves the book and marks the position; a fill books the position and fees first.
5. It calls the strategy hook, such as `on_book` or `on_fill`. The hook calls `ctx.set_quotes`, which only records the wanted quotes.
6. The quote manager compares the wanted quotes with the resting orders and produces new, cancel and replace messages.
7. Each new order and replace passes the pre-trade risk checks ([Risk model](risk-model.md)). A refused order is never sent.
8. The surviving messages are journaled and handed to the network thread, which encodes, signs and writes them.
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-how-it-works#5: The venue's acknowledgement or fill comes back the same way and re-enters at step 3. Each step in detail: [Event flow](event-flow.md).
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-how-it-works#6:
| Guarantee | Why it holds | Where it stops |
|---|---|---|
| A refused order is never sent | the risk check runs on the engine thread before the order reaches the network thread | limits you did not set are not checked; a limit of `0` is off |
| Cancels always go out | the risk checks pass cancels, also while the kill switch is set | the venue can still refuse or lose one |
| Every event is recorded before it is acted on | the engine journals an event before it dispatches it | the record reaches a queue, not the disk ([durability](../how-to/operations/running-in-production.md#durability)) |
| A replay sends the same orders | clock, events, orders and randomness come from the journal ([Determinism](determinism.md)) | needs the same binary and the recorded configuration |
| Order events are never dropped | a full order-event queue trips the kill switch and ends the session with exit code 5 | a full market-data queue drops the update and resyncs the book |
| Client order ids are unique across restarts | `[engine] epoch_file` counts sessions into the upper half of the id | lose the file and ids repeat |
| The engine does not allocate while trading | all its memory is reserved at start-up ([Memory](architecture.md#memory)) | with `spin_mode = "adaptive"` the engine sleeps when idle |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-how-it-works#7:
| Topic | What happens |
|---|---|
| Restart | the position comes back from the store, the kill switch and `max_loss` budget from `<engine>.kill`; old open orders are cancelled and books rebuilt from snapshots before the first order |
| Fills missed while the private stream was down | each connector replays the trade history before reconciling, and once a minute after that |
| Several settlement currencies | `[accounting]` converts PnL, `max_loss` and exposure caps to one reporting currency; without it, mixed currencies with `max_loss` set refuse to start |
| Monitoring | the status file, `fastmm-top` and its Prometheus endpoint, every 250 ms ([Monitor a session](../how-to/operations/monitor-with-fastmm-top.md)) |
| Risk across processes | `max_loss` and the notional caps cover one session; `fastmm-gateway`'s `[gateway]` limits cover the account |
| Venue margin, balance and position limits | the venue enforces them; its rejection is an ordinary reject |
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-how-it-works#8: What to set for each row: [Run in production](../how-to/operations/running-in-production.md).
chunks.fastmm-docs-explanation-how-it-works#9:
The engine is one template built three ways, so a strategy's source is the same in all of them:

| | Clock | Events | Orders |
|---|---|---|---|
| Backtest | simulated, from event times | a generator, a journal or a CSV file | an in-process matching engine with a latency model |
| Replay | the recorded engine clock | the journal, in recorded order | the recorded acknowledgements |
| Live | CPU counter calibrated to wall time | the network threads' queues | the venue |
